claims.claim: The nervous system is the system of neurons, nerves, tracts, and associated tissues that, together with the endocrine system, coordinates the activities of the organism in response to signals from internal and external environments (the basis of this lesson's working definition of the nervous system as the body's rapid communication network).

The nervous system can be divided into two major subdivisions: the central nervous system (CNS), comprised of the brain and spinal cord, and the peripheral nervous system (PNS), which connects the CNS to the rest of the body.

The central nervous system is the entire complex of neurons, axons, and supporting tissue that constitutes the brain and spinal cord, and it is primarily involved in mental activities and in coordinating and integrating incoming sensory messages and outgoing motor messages.

The peripheral nervous system is the portion of the nervous system outside the brain and spinal cord; afferent fibers bring messages from the sense organs to the CNS and efferent fibers transmit messages from the CNS to the muscles and glands.
Sensory nerves bring messages in and motor nerves send messages out to the muscles and organs, and messages travel to and from the brain (the two-way traffic account).
The neuron is the basic cellular unit of the nervous system; neurons serve as interconnected information processors essential for all of the tasks of the nervous system.
The cerebrum is the largest part of the brain, and the cerebral cortex is associated with higher-level processes such as consciousness, thought, emotion, reasoning, language, and memory.

The cerebellum modulates muscular contractions to produce smooth, accurately timed movements and receives messages from muscles, tendons, joints, and the ear to control balance, coordination, movement, and motor skills.
The brainstem is the part of the brain that connects the cerebrum with the spinal cord; the medulla, pons, and related structures control basic processes of life such as breathing and digestion.

Neuroplasticity (neural plasticity) is the ability of the nervous system to change in response to experience or environmental stimulation; it can occur through personal experiences, developmental processes, or in response to damage or injury.
The nervous system is most plastic when we are very young, yet it remains capable of remarkable changes later in life.
Biopsychology explores how biology, especially the nervous system, influences behavior — the basis of the lesson's honest framing that the brain is the hardware the mind runs on.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is the nervous system 'the brain,' or something larger?
positions: Lay usage often treats 'nervous system' and 'brain' as the same thing
The standard account divides the nervous system into the CNS (brain and spinal cord) and the PNS, which reaches the whole body (OpenStax 3.3; APA Dictionary)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson presents the brain as one organ within the larger nervous system and names the two divisions explicitly, so readers can tell the whole network from its central organ.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Does neuroplasticity mean the brain can recover fully from any damage?
positions: Popular accounts imply the brain can regenerate or fully repair itself

Authoritative definitions describe change and adaptation in response to experience or stimulation, including reorganization after injury, without promising full regeneration (APA Dictionary; OpenStax 3.4)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson defines plasticity as change and adaptation and notes in Common Mistakes that it is not unlimited regeneration.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is the mind simply the brain?
positions: A purely biological reading reduces mental life to nervous-system tissue
Psychology's working definition is the scientific study of the mind and behavior, studied at their own level as well (OpenStax 1.1; 1.3)
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The honest framing states that the brain is the hardware mental life runs on, while noting the hardware does not by itself explain the meaning of thoughts or choices.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft contained only generic boilerplate ('Brain And Nervous System is a foundational concept in Psychology...') with no factual claims to preserve; all substantive content was written from verified sources.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the machine-generated boilerplate draft entirely with source-verified original prose.
Attributed the working definition of the nervous system to the APA Dictionary of Psychology rather than presenting it as common knowledge.
Attributed neuroplasticity to both the APA Dictionary (neural plasticity entry) and OpenStax Psychology 2e 3.4, and stated its limits rather than treating it as unlimited regeneration.
